Cell Structure & Interactions the cell's scaffold, its surroundings, and the joins between

Dr Annika van Hummel's four-part series, decoded end to end — the cytoskeleton that holds a cell in shape and moves it, the extracellular matrix it lives in, and the junctions that lock cells to each other and to that matrix. Built from the lecture's own figures.

Covers Parts 1–4 · 52 slides Figures 28 plates from your slides Depth reasoning + clinical

How to use this guide

Every subsection has a reference code like §8.1 — quote it to go deeper on exactly that piece. Each figure from your slides appears as a numbered Plate with a Label Key decoding every labelled part. The coloured tags carry the extras:

Reasoning
The why behind the structure — form follows function.

A trick to lock it in for the exam.

What it means when it fails.
§0Orientation · why these four lectures belong together

Inside, outside, and in between

A tissue is not a bag of cells — it is cells plus the material between them, held in a shape.

Dr van Hummel's title pairs two words on purpose: structure and interactions. A cell has to do three physical jobs at once, and the four parts of this series take them in turn.

  1. Hold its own shape and move — done by an internal protein scaffold, the cytoskeleton (Parts 1–2, our §1–§6).
  2. Build and sit inside its surroundings — the extracellular matrix (ECM), the material cells secrete around themselves (Part 3, our §7–§9).
  3. Stick to its neighbours and to that matrix — cell junctions, the specialised joins (Part 4, our §10–§12).

Read in that order the series has a clean logic: inside → outside → the connections between. Everything downstream is a variation on one theme — proteins that either resist force, generate force, or transmit force from one place to another.

Reasoning · why teach structure and interactions as one topic

Because they are mechanically continuous. An integrin in the cell membrane grips a matrix protein outside the cell and, through adaptor proteins, an actin filament inside it — so a pull on the tissue is felt all the way to the nucleus, and a cell's internal tension is felt out in the matrix. You cannot understand the cytoskeleton without where it anchors, or the matrix without what grips it. The junctions are simply where the inside scaffold and the outside matrix are wired together.

Clinical / real-world · one failure, three systems

Think of cancer metastasis as the whole of this series going wrong at once: a tumour cell rebuilds its cytoskeleton to crawl (§6.2), secretes proteases to chew through the matrix (§9), loosens its cell–cell junctions to break away (§11), and re-grips new matrix with integrins (§12). Every mechanism below is a step a cancer cell subverts — which is exactly why they are worth understanding as a set.

Memory hook · the spine of the series

Scaffold → Surroundings → Stitches.

Cytoskeleton is the scaffold; the ECM is the surroundings; junctions are the stitches that sew scaffold to surroundings and cell to cell.

§1Part 1 · cytoskeleton overview · slides 3–5

The cytoskeleton: three filament systems

One scaffold, three cables — each a different polymer for a different job.

Cells must organise themselves in space and interact mechanically with their environment. They do it with a system of protein filaments — the cytoskeleton — that lets them grow, divide, adapt and move. There are three filament types, and the whole of Parts 1–2 is spent on them and their helpers.

Label Key — reading Plate 1.1 across the three columns
Microfilaments (actin)
Subunit: actin monomer. Diameter ~7–9 nm — the thinnest. Job: shape the cell surface and drive locomotion. The fluorescence image shows them concentrated at the cell edge.
Microtubules
Subunit: the αβ-tubulin dimer. Diameter ~25 nm — the thickest and stiffest, a hollow tube. Job: position organelles and act as transport tracks; they radiate from a central point.
Intermediate filaments
Subunit: various (keratins, vimentin, lamins…). Diameter ~10 nm — intermediate between the other two, which is how they are named. Job: pure mechanical strength; they form a basket through the cytoplasm.

As Plate 1.1 makes clear, the three are told apart first by thickness (7–9 nm → 10 nm → 25 nm) and then by what they are for. Commit the division of labour now — every later section is a detail of one of these three:

The three filaments at a glance
FilamentSubunitDiameterPolarity?Chief role
Actin microfilamentGlobular actin (+ ATP)7–9 nmYes (+/−)Cell-surface shape & movement (crawling, contraction)
Microtubuleαβ-tubulin dimer (+ GTP)25 nmYes (+/−)Organelle position & intracellular transport tracks
Intermediate filamentVarious fibrous proteins~10 nmNoMechanical strength — resisting tension

§1.1Dynamic by design — and why polarity matters

Filaments are dynamic and adaptable: a given structure may last less than a minute or the whole life of the cell. Each is built from large numbers of small subunits that diffuse rapidly through the cytosol (the big polymer cannot). That design is the whole trick — subunits can disassemble in one place and reassemble elsewhere in seconds, letting the cell re-plumb its entire skeleton on demand. Cell polarity — which end is "front" — is set by how the cytoskeleton is configured.

Reasoning · why build a skeleton out of loose bricks?

A welded steel frame is strong but permanent; the cell needs strength and the ability to completely reorganise for mitosis, crawling or repair. Building from a pool of small, diffusible subunits solves both: the polymer is load-bearing while assembled, yet a change in signalling tips the equilibrium toward disassembly and the bricks scatter to be reused. This is why the same cell can be a flat, spread fibroblast one hour and a rounded dividing cell the next (you will see exactly this in Plate 6.1).

Label Key — Plate 1.2 (colour legend at the foot of the figure)
Actin microfilaments
Red. Fill the microvilli at the apical surface and form the terminal web just beneath — the cell's surface-shaping mesh.
Microtubules
Green. Run apical→basal through the cell with defined + and − ends marked — the long-distance tracks.
Intermediate filaments
Blue. Form a basket around the nucleus and tie into the desmosomes — the tension-bearing net.
Junction preview
Adherens junction & desmosome (cell–cell) and hemidesmosome onto the basal lamina (cell–matrix) — the anchor points we return to in §11–§12. Note which filament each ties to.

Plate 1.2 is worth lingering on because it is the whole series in one picture: actin (red) shapes the surface, microtubules (green) cross the cell as tracks, intermediate filaments (blue) bear tension into the desmosomes, and the bottom of the cell is stitched to the basal lamina — a piece of ECM — by a hemidesmosome. Structure (the filaments) and interactions (the junctions) are already inseparable.

Memory hook · what each filament is for

Actin Acts, Microtubules Move things, Intermediates hold the line.

Actin = Action (shape change, crawling); Microtubules = Motorways (transport & organelle position); Intermediate = Iron rebar (tensile strength). Thickness runs in the opposite order to the alphabet: thinnest actin, thickest microtubule.

Clinical / real-world · the cytoskeleton is a drug target and a disease site

Because these filaments are essential and dynamic, they are heavily drugged and frequently broken: anti-cancer drugs freeze microtubules to block mitosis (§3), toxins and lab tools poison actin (§2), and inherited mutations in intermediate filaments cause blistering skin and muscle disease (§4). Keep a running list as we go — each filament has its own clinical signature.

§2Part 1 · microfilaments · slides 6–9

Microfilaments — actin

A polar double helix of ATP-loaded beads, re-woven into whatever shape the surface needs.

Actin is the thinnest filament and the one that shapes the cell surface and drives crawling. Start with the single building block, then see how binding proteins weave it into completely different structures.

Label Key — Plate 2.1
Actin monomer (A)
A single globular (G-)actin protein with a molecule of ATP bound in its central cleft (it becomes ADP once buried in a filament). This is the brick.
ATP / ADP
The bound nucleotide is a timer: freshly added subunits carry ATP; older, internal ones have hydrolysed it to ADP — marking them for release. Drives the dynamics.
Filament (B)
Two protofilaments wound into a double helix. Because every subunit points the same way, the filament is polar.
Plus (+) / barbed end
The fast-growing end — monomers add here preferentially. "Barbed" comes from the arrowhead pattern myosin makes when it decorates the filament.
Minus (−) / pointed end
The slow end, where subunits tend to leave.

Trace Plate 2.1 left to right: a globular monomer with central ATP → two protofilaments twisted into a double helix → the polar filament with a plus (barbed) and minus (pointed) end. Polymerisation needs a starting seed: three monomers form a trimer that acts as a stable nucleus onto which more monomers add — the process of nucleation. Nucleation is the slow, rate-limiting step, which is exactly why the cell controls it with dedicated proteins.

Reasoning · why polarity + an ATP timer = directional growth (treadmilling)

Because the two ends differ and the nucleotide marks a subunit's age, a filament can add ATP-actin at the plus end while losing ADP-actin from the minus end at the same rate — the filament stays the same length but subunits flux through it, a behaviour called treadmilling. That directional turnover is how actin pushes a membrane forward: net growth at the plus end (pointed at the leading edge) physically extends the cell. Polarity is not a detail — it is the arrow that tells the filament which way to push.

Label Key — Plate 2.2 (the four arrays and where they sit)
Stress fibre → contractile bundle
Loosely packed, mixed-polarity actin with myosin — contracts. Pulls the cell body forward and exerts tension on adhesions.
Cell cortex → gel-like network
A criss-cross mesh just under the membrane — gives the surface its stiffness and shape.
Lamellipodium → dendritic (branched) network
A branched sheet at the leading edge; its plus-end growth pushes the membrane out as the cell crawls.
Filopodium → tight parallel bundle
Tightly bundled parallel filaments forming finger-like probes that sense the surroundings.

The same monomer, organised by actin-binding proteins, becomes four different machines — shown in Plate 2.2. Which array forms depends on the nucleation protein: different nucleators build different geometries (branched for a lamellipodium, parallel for a filopodium, anti-parallel with myosin for a contractile bundle). This is the payoff of the trimer/nucleation step in §2 — control nucleation and you control the shape.

Memory hook · which end is which

Plus = Barbed & Busy; Minus = Pointed & Poky.

The Plus end is Barbed and busy (fast-growing, at the leading edge). The minus end is Pointed and grows poorly. "Barbed/pointed" come from the myosin-decoration arrowheads in the EM panels of Plate 2.1.

Clinical / real-world · actin as a toxin target and a metastasis engine

Actin dynamics are so central that many natural toxins hit them — phalloidin (death-cap mushroom) locks filaments, cytochalasins cap the plus end and latrunculin sequesters monomers; all three are standard lab tools precisely because they paralyse the cell. Clinically, the branched lamellipodial and filopodial arrays of Plate 2.2 are the very machinery a metastasising cancer cell switches on to crawl out of a tumour (§6.2) — reactivated developmental motility in the wrong place.

§3Part 1 · microtubules · slides 10–12

Microtubules

Stiff hollow tubes that grow and collapse on a knife-edge, all radiating from one organising centre.

Microtubules are the thickest, stiffest filament — hollow cylinders of tubulin. They set where organelles sit and serve as the tracks motor proteins run on (§5). Two ideas define them: dynamic instability and the MTOC.

Label Key — Plate 3.1
Hollow cylinder, 25 nm
Made of the protein tubulin; the hollow tube is far more rigid than actin — why it works as a compression-resistant strut and a straight track.
Triplet cross-section
At the base of cilia and in centrioles, microtubules occur as rings of triplets — the "9-triplet" arrangement of the centriole.
Interphase array (green)
In a resting cell, microtubules radiate outward from near the nucleus, positioning organelles (red) — the "delivery map".
Ciliated protozoan
Surface microtubule-based cilia — a preview of §6.3.

Plate 3.1 shows the essentials: a hollow 25 nm tube of tubulin, straight and stiff, usually anchored at a microtubule-organising centre. The building block is the αβ-tubulin dimer, and — as with actin — a bound nucleotide runs the dynamics, but here it is GTP.

Label Key — Plate 3.2
GTP "T-form" = plus end
Tubulin carrying GTP adds to the plus end. A cap of GTP-tubulin stabilises the tip and lets it grow.
GDP "D-form" = minus end / core
Once buried, GTP is hydrolysed to GDP; GDP-tubulin wants to peel apart, so if the cap is lost the microtubule rapidly shrinks.
Growing vs shrinking (EM)
The two micrographs show a straight, capped growing tip versus a frayed, splaying shrinking end — the two states the same microtubule flips between.

Microtubules are dynamically unstable: an individual tube flips, seemingly at random, between growing and abruptly shrinking. As Plate 3.2 shows, the switch is the GTP cap — GTP-tubulin ("T-form") adds at the plus end and holds the tip together; when hydrolysis catches up and the cap is lost, the GDP core ("D-form") springs apart and the tube collapses.

Reasoning · why would a cell want an unstable skeleton?

Dynamic instability is a search strategy. Microtubules grow out in all directions, and most collapse — but any that happen to hit and bind a target (a chromosome's kinetochore during mitosis, or a specific patch of cortex) are captured and stabilised. This "search-and-capture" lets the cell explore its whole interior cheaply and wire up the mitotic spindle without a blueprint. The instability is the mechanism, not a flaw.

Label Key — Plate 3.3
Centrosome / MTOC
The microtubule-organising centre — where microtubules are nucleated. The minus ends are anchored here; plus ends point outward.
Interphase cell
A single aster of microtubules fans out from the centrosome to position organelles.
Mitotic cell / spindle poles
In division the MTOC duplicates to form the two spindle poles that segregate chromosomes.
Neurone
Microtubules run the length of the axon; the minus ends orient back toward the cell body — the basis of axonal transport (§5).
Cilium/flagellum — basal body
Here the organising centre is a basal body at the cell surface, templating the axoneme (§6.3).

Microtubules do not float free — they are assembled from microtubule-organising centres (MTOCs). Plate 3.3 shows the same principle in four settings: the interphase aster, the mitotic spindle, the neuron's axon and the cilium's basal body. The rule to carry forward: in all cases except dendrites, the minus (−) end is anchored at or oriented toward the MTOC, with plus ends pointing out. That fixed geometry is what makes directional transport possible in §5.

Memory hook · which nucleotide, which end

GTP = "Grow To Plus."

GTP-tubulin adds at the plus end and lets it grow; lose the GTP cap and the GDP core goes. (Actin uses ATP, microtubules use GTP — the thicker filament, the "G".)

Clinical / real-world · the mitosis drugs — and a dementia link

Because the spindle is pure microtubule, it is a prime chemotherapy target: taxanes (paclitaxel) over-stabilise microtubules and vinca alkaloids (vincristine) destabilise them — either way a dividing cell cannot build a working spindle and dies. Colchicine (gout) works the same way on neutrophils. And close to Dr van Hummel's own field: the microtubule-stabilising protein tau comes loose and aggregates in Alzheimer's disease and other tauopathies — when tau leaves the microtubules, axonal transport fails and the neuron degenerates.

§4Part 2 · intermediate filaments · slides 3–4

Intermediate filaments

The rope with no ends — no polarity, no motors, pure tensile strength.

The third filament is the odd one out. Actin and microtubules are polar dynamic tracks; intermediate filaments (IFs) are ropelike, ~10 nm, non-polar cables whose only job is mechanical strength. They are the reason a sheet of skin can be stretched without its cells tearing apart.

Label Key — Plate 4.1 (assembly, step by step)
(A) α-helical monomer
A single elongated protein with an α-helical rod domain — not a compact globule like actin/tubulin. Sets up a rope, not a bead-string.
(B) Coiled-coil dimer
Two monomers wrap around each other (~48 nm) — the basic unit.
(C) Staggered tetramer
Two dimers align antiparallel and staggered. Because they point opposite ways, the tetramer has no overall direction — this is where IF polarity is cancelled.
Lateral association of 8 tetramers
Eight tetramers pack side-by-side into the mature rope, giving it its thickness and strength.
Growing filament
Tetramers add along the length — the finished ~10 nm rope, like a many-stranded cable.

Follow Plate 4.1: α-helical monomer → coiled-coil dimer → antiparallel, staggered tetramer → eight tetramers packed side-by-side → rope. The critical step is the antiparallel tetramer: because half the subunits point each way, the finished filament has no plus or minus end. That single fact explains everything distinctive about IFs.

Reasoning · why "no polarity" makes IFs the tension-bearer

No polarity means no nucleotide, no treadmilling, and no motor proteins — nothing walks along an intermediate filament, and it does not grow directionally. What it gains in exchange is toughness under tension: a rope of many staggered, laterally bonded strands can be stretched hard and stubbornly resist breaking, sharing load along its whole length. Actin and microtubules snap or buckle under sustained pull; IFs are built to take it. Form follows function — the "boring" architecture is the point.

Label Key — Plate 4.2
Neurofilaments
The IFs of nerve-cell axons — set axon calibre and mechanical resilience.
Cytoplasmic meshwork
IFs span the cytoplasm from one cell–cell junction to another, tying the whole epithelium into a shared mechanical unit.
Nuclear lamina
A special IF meshwork (the lamins) lining the inner nuclear envelope — mechanical support for the nucleus and organisation of chromatin.

IFs are a large, heterogeneous family — different tissues express different members, which is clinically useful because a tumour often keeps the IF type of its tissue of origin (pathologists stain for them). Learn the four groups and where each lives:

Major types of intermediate filament (Part 2, slide 4 table)
ClassExample proteinsWhere
NuclearLamins A, B, CNuclear lamina (inner nuclear envelope) of all cells
Vimentin-likeVimentin; desmin; glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP); peripherinConnective tissue & mesenchyme; muscle; glia (astrocytes); some neurons
EpithelialKeratins (acidic type I & neutral/basic type II)Epithelia and derivatives — skin, hair, nails
AxonalNeurofilament proteins (NF-L, NF-M, NF-H)Neurons (axons)
Memory hook · the odd one out

Intermediate = "Inert & Iron": no ends, no engine, just strength.

If a question hinges on polarity, GTP/ATP or motor transport, the answer is not intermediate filaments. Their whole identity is: non-polar, non-dynamic, tension-bearing.

Clinical / real-world · when the rope frays

Every IF class has a disease of mechanical failure. Keratin mutations cause epidermolysis bullosa simplex — the skin blisters from minor friction because basal cells rupture. Desmin mutations give a myopathy/cardiomyopathy; lamin mutations cause progeria and other "laminopathies" (a fragile nucleus); GFAP causes Alexander disease. And accumulating neurofilaments are a hallmark of neurodegeneration such as ALS — indeed, neurofilament light chain in blood/CSF is now a biomarker of neuronal damage.

§5Part 2 · accessory & motor proteins · slides 5–7

Motor & accessory proteins

The filaments are the roads; these proteins are the traffic controllers and the trucks.

Filaments alone are inert. Accessory proteins regulate their number, geometry, length, stability and attachments; a special class — motor proteins — bind a polar filament and walk along it, burning ATP, to haul cargo or generate force.

§5.1Accessory proteins — the regulators

Cells regulate the cytoskeleton by controlling how filaments attach to one another and to other cell components; this is the job of regulatory accessory proteins (the nucleators of §2 are one example). Motor proteins are the subset that move: most carry membrane-enclosed organelles — mitochondria, Golgi stacks, secretory vesicles — to their correct locations, while others make filaments exert tension or slide against each other to generate force (muscle contraction, cell division).

Label Key — Plate 5.1
Head
The motor domain — binds and hydrolyses ATP and grips actin. Each stroke walks it one step toward the plus end.
Neck / hinge + light chains
A lever arm; its length sets the step size. Light chains stiffen and regulate it.
Coiled-coil tail (~150 nm)
Two heavy chains wound together; the tail dimerises myosins and carries the cargo or forms filaments.
Class I (step 10–14 nm)
Single-headed; associates directly with membranes (endocytosis, membrane tension).
Class II (step 8 nm)
The muscle myosin — assembles into bipolar filaments that pull antiparallel actin together to contract.
Class V (step 36 nm)
Long-necked, big steps — an organelle-transport motor that walks vesicles along actin.

Plate 5.1 decodes myosin: a head that binds and hydrolyses ATP to "walk" toward actin's plus end, a neck lever with light chains, and a coiled-coil tail. The lecture names three classes — Class I (membrane association/endocytosis), Class II (muscle contraction), and Class III (interacting with organelle receptors); the figure illustrates the family with Class I, II and V, where the long-stepping Class V is the organelle carrier. The theme: same motor head, different tail and neck for different jobs.

Label Key — Plate 5.2
Kinesin → plus end (anterograde)
Walks cargo toward the plus end — outward, away from the MTOC (in a neuron, down the axon: anterograde).
Cytoplasmic dynein → minus end (retrograde)
Walks cargo toward the minus end — inward, toward the MTOC/cell body (retrograde).
Dynactin
An adaptor complex that links dynein to its cargo and boosts its processivity.
Cell transport map
Shows the two motors distributing organelles (ER, Golgi, endosomes, mitochondria, secretory vesicles) to their proper addresses.

Both microtubule motors — kinesins and dyneins — burn ATP (ATP → ADP) to transport cargo, but in opposite directions, as Plate 5.2 shows. This is where the fixed MTOC geometry of §3 pays off.

Reasoning · why polarity + directional motors = an addressing system

Because a microtubule is polar and each motor runs only one way, "plus-end" and "minus-end" become addresses. With minus ends anchored at the MTOC (near the nucleus) and plus ends at the periphery, kinesin = outbound and dynein = inbound. In a metre-long motor neuron this is life-or-death: kinesin ships fresh mitochondria and vesicles down the axon (anterograde), dynein returns worn components and injury signals back to the soma (retrograde). Muscle contraction is the same trick in a different key — Class II myosin sliding antiparallel actin to shorten the fibre.

Memory hook · which motor, which way

"Kinesin walKs to the + and Kicks cargo out; Dynein Draws it Down to the −."

Kinesin → plus/periphery (anterograde). Dynein → minus/centre (retrograde). Myosin is the actin motor and (almost always) walks to actin's plus end.

Clinical / real-world · broken motors

Motor failure is neurologically and cardiologically loud. Defects in axonal transport (kinesin/dynein) feature in ALS, Charcot–Marie–Tooth and other neurodegenerations — the far ends of long axons starve first. Cardiac β-myosin (MYH7) mutations cause hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, a leading cause of sudden death in young athletes. The unifying lesson: a cell the size of a neuron or the power of a heart cell cannot survive on diffusion — it lives or dies by its motors.

§6Part 2 · the cytoskeleton at work · slides 8–10

The cytoskeleton in action

Three whole-cell behaviours — dividing, crawling, beating — all from the same three filaments and their motors.

Now watch the parts assemble. Cell division, cell migration and the beating of cilia are just the filaments of §1–§5 re-deployed in space and time.

§6.1Cell division

Label Key — Plate 6.1 (the four numbered stages)
1 — Interphase
A spread fibroblast: actin (red) spread across the base, microtubules (green) radiating from the MTOC.
2 — Mitosis
Actin disassembles so the cell rounds up and stops moving; microtubules reconfigure into the mitotic spindle.
3 — Cytokinesis
An actin contractile ring forms round the equator and pinches the cell into two.
4 — Two daughters
Actin and microtubules rebuild their interphase arrangements in two flattened, smaller daughter cells.

Plate 6.1 is the payoff of §1.1's "loose bricks" argument: within one cell cycle, actin and microtubules completely tear down and rebuild. Microtubules abandon the interphase aster to become the spindle; actin abandons its spread arrays to become a contractile ring. Same subunits, new machines.

§6.2Cell migration

Label Key — Plate 6.2 (the crawl cycle)
Step 1 — Extension
The cell pushes out a lamellipodium at its leading edge — the branched actin array of Plate 2.2 growing against the membrane.
Step 2 — Adhesion
The lamellipodium sticks down via focal adhesions — integrin-based links between the actin cytoskeleton and ECM proteins (§12).
Step 3 — Translocation
Actin–myosin II stress fibres at the rear contract and drag the bulk of the cytoplasm forward.
Step 4 — De-adhesion
The tail releases (de-adhesion + endocytic recycling of adhesion components); contraction retracts it into the body.

Cells migrate during development, wound healing, immune responses and cancer metastasis. Plate 6.2 shows the universal cycle: protrude (lamellipodial actin) → grip (focal adhesions) → pull (stress-fibre contraction) → release (rear de-adhesion). Notice how many earlier pieces converge here — the branched array of §2, the myosin motor of §5, and the integrin adhesions of §12.

Reasoning · why crawling needs adhesion, not just pushing

A lamellipodium pushing on the membrane would just fold back on itself unless the cell could get traction. Focal adhesions provide it: they are the cell's crampons, transiently gripping the matrix so contraction has something to pull against. That is why migration couples the cytoskeleton (this section) to cell–matrix junctions (§12) — movement is impossible without a grip to move against. The rear must then let go, or the cell tears itself apart, so migration is an ordered cycle of grip-front / release-back.

§6.3Cilia & flagella

Label Key — Plate 6.3
Flagellum vs cilium (beat)
Flagella (sperm, protozoa) beat with a snake-like wave to swim through liquid; cilia beat with a whip-like power-and-recovery stroke to move liquid over a cell surface.
Axoneme "9+2"
The core: nine outer doublet microtubules around a central pair. This is the microtubule-based engine.
Dynein arms
Motor arms between adjacent doublets. They try to slide doublets past each other; because the doublets are tethered, sliding is converted into bending — the beat.
Radial spokes / links
Connect doublets to the centre and to each other, constraining sliding so it becomes a controlled bend.

Cilia and flagella are hairlike appendages built from microtubules and dynein. As Plate 6.3 shows, movement comes from bending of the core, the axoneme: dynein arms slide the nine outer doublets against each other, and because the doublets are linked, sliding becomes a bend. In the airway, ciliary beating sweeps a layer of mucus — with trapped dust and bacteria — up toward the mouth to be cleared.

Clinical / real-world · when cilia can't beat

Mutations in the axonemal dynein arms cause primary ciliary dyskinesia (Kartagener syndrome): immotile cilia mean recurrent chest infections and bronchiectasis (mucus is never cleared), infertility (sperm can't swim; fallopian cilia can't move the ovum) and situs inversus in ~50% (embryonic nodal cilia set left–right body asymmetry, and without them it is a coin-toss). One broken motor, a whole syndrome — a vivid illustration of §5's theme. The same clearance escalator is what chronic smoking paralyses.

Memory hook · the axoneme

"9 + 2, and dynein makes it do."

Nine outer doublets + two central singlets = 9+2. The motor that bends it is the same dynein family from §5 — here anchored, converting sliding into a beat.

R Recall checklist — the cytoskeleton (Parts 1–2)
  • Three filaments — actin (7–9 nm, shape/movement), microtubules (25 nm, transport/positioning), intermediate filaments (10 nm, strength).
  • Actin — polar double helix of ATP-actin; plus/barbed vs minus/pointed end; nucleation via a trimer; binding proteins build cortex, lamellipodia, filopodia, stress fibres.
  • Microtubules — hollow 25 nm tubes of αβ-tubulin; dynamic instability via a GTP cap; nucleated at the MTOC with minus ends anchored there.
  • Intermediate filaments — non-polar staggered ropes; no nucleotide, no motors; keratin/vimentin/desmin/GFAP/neurofilaments/lamins.
  • Motors — myosin walks actin (to +); kinesin (to +, anterograde) and dynein (to −, retrograde) walk microtubules; all use ATP.
  • Whole-cell jobs — division (spindle + actin contractile ring), migration (protrude/adhere/contract/release), cilia/flagella (9+2 axoneme bent by dynein).
  • Clinical anchors — taxanes/vinca & tau (microtubules); phalloidin & metastasis (actin); epidermolysis bullosa & ALS-neurofilaments (IFs); Kartagener (dynein).
§7Part 3 · extracellular matrix · slides 3–5

The extracellular matrix — ground substance

The material cells live in — a charged, water-swollen gel that shrugs off compression.

Step outside the cell. The extracellular matrix (ECM) is the material between cells, and it makes up a large fraction of most tissues — cartilage is nearly all matrix with few cells; the brain is nearly all cells with little matrix. Crucially, the ECM is made and organised locally by the very cells that sit in it. It has two great classes of molecule: gel-forming glycosaminoglycans/proteoglycans (this section) and fibrous proteins (§8).

Label Key — Plate 7.1
Chondrocyte
The cartilage cell that secretes the surrounding matrix — cells make their own environment.
Proteoglycan aggregate
Enormous, bottle-brush complexes of GAGs on protein cores (detailed in Plate 7.2) — the water-holding component.
Collagen fibril
The tensile mesh (§8) that cages the swelling gel so it builds pressure rather than simply expanding.

§7.1Glycosaminoglycans (GAGs) — the gel

GAGs are unbranched polysaccharide chains of repeating disaccharide units. They are highly negatively charged and hydrophilic, so they flop into extended shapes that occupy a huge volume for their mass and form gels. That dense negative charge pulls in cations (especially Na⁺), which osmotically drag in large amounts of water — giving the matrix its ability to withstand compressive forces, as in the cartilage of the knee (Plate 7.1). There are four main groups:

  • Hyaluronan — the giant exception: not sulfated, not attached to a protein core.
  • Chondroitin sulfate — abundant in cartilage.
  • Heparan sulfate — cell-surface signalling co-receptor (and the anticoagulant heparin is a relative).
  • Keratan sulfate — cartilage, cornea.
Worked reasoning · why a sugar gel can bear your body weight

The claim on the slide — GAGs "withstand compressive forces" — is really a short physics argument. Trace it:

  1. Fixed negative charge. Every few sugars carries a COO⁻ or SO₃⁻ group. These charges are stuck to the chain — they cannot diffuse away.
  2. Counter-ions crowd in. To balance that fixed charge, mobile cations (mostly Na⁺) accumulate in the matrix — so the ion concentration inside the gel far exceeds that outside.
  3. Water follows by osmosis. High internal solute → water is drawn in, and the gel swells until the inward osmotic pull is balanced by the tension of the surrounding collagen mesh (Plate 7.1).
  4. Result — a pressurised cushion. The trapped water is nearly incompressible, so a load on the knee is resisted by fluid pressure, not by crushing the tissue. Squeeze it and water is forced out; release and it osmotically re-swells.

Compression resistance = fixed anionic charge → Na⁺ → osmotic water uptake → a turgid, collagen-caged cushion. Lose the GAGs (osteoarthritis) and the cushion deflates.

§7.2Proteoglycans — GAGs on a core

Label Key — Plate 7.2
Core protein
The protein backbone a set of GAG chains is covalently attached to — one proteoglycan.
GAG side chains
Keratan- and chondroitin-sulfate chains bristling off the core — the "brush" that holds water.
Hyaluronan backbone
A single long hyaluronan onto which many proteoglycans dock, making a giant aggregate (e.g. aggrecan, >100 GAG chains).

All GAGs except hyaluronan are covalently attached to a protein core to form proteoglycans — and these have almost limitless arrangements. As Plate 7.2 shows, dozens of proteoglycans dock onto one hyaluronan to build an aggregate the size of a bacterium (aggrecan, the main proteoglycan of cartilage, carries >100 GAG chains). Beyond water-holding, proteoglycans also act as a selective sieve, in chemical signalling, as regulators of proteolytic enzymes, and as cell-surface co-receptors.

Reasoning · division of labour with the fibres

The ECM solves two opposite mechanical problems with two different molecules. Compression (a squashing load, as in a joint) is resisted by the hydrated GAG gel pushing back with fluid pressure. Tension (a stretching load, as in a tendon) is resisted by collagen fibres (§8). A tissue tunes its ratio of the two to its mechanical brief — cartilage is gel-rich, tendon is fibre-rich. Same toolkit, different mix.

Memory hook · the four GAGs & the odd one out

"Healthy Cartilage Has Karate" → Hyaluronan, Chondroitin, Heparan, Keratan.

And remember the exception: Hyaluronan is the loner — no sulfate, no core protein, and it forms the backbone the others hang from.

Clinical / real-world · deflated cushions & clogged lysosomes

In osteoarthritis, aggrecan and GAGs are lost from joint cartilage, so it can no longer hold water or resist compression — the surface erodes and bone grinds on bone. At the other extreme, if the enzymes that degrade GAGs are missing (the mucopolysaccharidoses, e.g. Hurler syndrome), GAGs accumulate in lysosomes throughout the body causing organomegaly, skeletal and neurological disease. And the GAG relative heparin is one of the most-used anticoagulant drugs.

§8Part 3 · fibrous proteins · slides 6–8

The ECM — fibres & glue

Collagen for strength, elastin for spring, fibronectin to stick it all to cells.

The second class of matrix molecule is the fibrous proteins. Three matter here: collagen (tensile strength), elastin (stretch and recoil) and fibronectin (the glue that binds matrix to cells).

§8.1Collagen — tensile strength

Label Key — Plate 8.1
α-chains
Three polypeptide α-chains — the human genome has 42 distinct α-chain genes, giving many collagen types.
Triple helix (collagen molecule)
The three chains wind into a long, stiff triple-stranded helix — collagen's defining feature.
Collagen fibril (10–300 nm)
Many molecules pack in a staggered array into a banded fibril.
Collagen fibre (several μm)
Fibrils bundle into fibres, oriented in each tissue to resist tension in the direction it is loaded.

Collagen gives tensile strength and is the most abundant protein in mammals (~25% of total protein mass) — the major structural component of skin and bone. Its signature is the long, stiff, triple-stranded helix, which — following Plate 8.1 — packs into fibrils (10–300 nm) and then fibres (several μm), laid down in whatever direction a tissue is pulled. There are many types; the ones to know:

Collagen types worth knowing (from the Part 3 table)
TypeFormWhere
IFibrillarSkin, bone, tendon, ligament — the workhorse (~90% of body collagen)
IIFibrillarCartilage (with aggrecan from §7)
IIIFibrillar (reticular)Loose connective tissue, blood vessels, granulation tissue
IVNetworkBasal lamina (§9) — a mesh, not a rope
VIIAnchoring fibrilsBeneath stratified epithelia — pins epidermis to dermis
Reasoning · why glycine every third residue is non-negotiable

Collagen's α-chains have the repeat Gly-X-Y (X often proline, Y often hydroxyproline). Glycine is the smallest amino acid — just an H side-chain — and it is the only residue small enough to sit at the crowded centre of the three-stranded helix where the chains pack tightest. Replace even one glycine with a bulkier residue and the helix kinks and weakens — which is exactly the molecular lesion in osteogenesis imperfecta. The hydroxyl groups (needing vitamin C to be added) then cross-link neighbouring helices for strength — no vitamin C, no cross-links, hence scurvy.

§8.2Elastin — stretch & recoil

Label Key — Plate 8.2
Elastin molecules + cross-links
Individual elastin molecules tied together by cross-links; under load the network stretches, and on release it recoils to its resting shape — like a rubber sheet.
Elastic lamina (aorta, red)
Concentric layers of elastin in the aortic wall (the aorta is ~50% elastin) — they store the pulse and release it between beats.
L (lumen)
The vessel lumen; the layered laminae ring it.

Many tissues must be strong and elastic — skin, blood vessels, lungs. Elastic fibres are >5× more extensible than a rubber band of the same cross-section; elastin, cross-linked into networks, is their main component, and the aorta is ~50% elastin (Plate 8.2). Elastin is often interwoven with stiff, inelastic collagen that acts as a safety rope, limiting how far the tissue can stretch before it would tear.

Clinical / real-world · when the spring fails

Elastic-fibre disease is largely vascular. In Marfan syndrome, mutated fibrillin (the scaffold elastin is laid on) weakens the aortic wall → progressive aortic root dilation and dissection. Loss of the collagen safety-rope in Ehlers–Danlos does the same. Williams syndrome (elastin gene deletion) causes arterial stenoses, and cigarette-smoke proteases degrading lung elastin produce emphysema — the recoil that empties the alveoli is lost.

§8.3Fibronectin — the glue

Label Key — Plate 8.3
Fibronectin
A large multidomain glycoprotein with binding sites for other matrix molecules and for cell-surface receptors — it lets the ECM attach to cells (the "glue").
Integrin
The transmembrane receptor in the plasma membrane that binds fibronectin outside and the cytoskeleton inside (§12).
Microfilaments (actin)
Integrins link fibronectin to the actin cytoskeleton; the cell pulls, stretching fibronectin so it polymerises into fibrils.
Collagen fibre / proteoglycan complex
The other matrix components fibronectin also binds, tying the whole ECM together.

The ECM contains many glycoproteins with multiple domains and specific binding sites; fibronectin is the key one — it allows the ECM to attach to cells. It circulates as a soluble form in blood and exists as insoluble fibrils on cells that carry fibronectin-binding integrins. As Plate 8.3 shows, integrins link fibronectin to the actin cytoskeleton; the cell's tension physically stretches fibronectin, exposing sites that let it bind more fibronectin and assemble into fibrils. It is a two-way mechanical relay — the direct link between §8 (matrix) and §12 (cell–matrix junctions).

Memory hook · the three fibrous jobs

Collagen = Cable · Elastin = Elastic band · Fibronectin = Fixative.

Collagen resists tension, Elastin gives recoil, Fibronectin glues matrix to cell. (Compression, meanwhile, is the GAG gel's job from §7.)

§9Part 3 · remodelling & basal lamina · slides 9–11

Remodelling & the basal lamina

The matrix is not permanent — cells constantly rebuild it, and one specialised sheet underlies every epithelium.

Cells both synthesise and degrade the ECM, and one thin, specialised form of it — the basal lamina — sits under every epithelium doing outsized work.

§9.1Making & degrading the matrix

Cells must break the matrix down as well as build it — to remodel tissues under stress (e.g. bone), to divide while embedded in matrix, and to travel through it (a white blood cell reaching an infection). Degradation is done by extracellular proteases, especially matrix metalloproteases (MMPs). Some are specific (e.g. collagenases), others broad; many are anchored to the plasma membrane so they only cut a defined patch of matrix. Because uncontrolled digestion would be catastrophic, activity is tightly controlled by (i) local activation — most are secreted inactive; (ii) confinement by cell-surface receptors; and (iii) protease inhibitors.

Reasoning · why keep proteases on such a tight leash?

An enzyme that cuts collagen is, unchecked, an enzyme that dissolves your tendons and vessel walls. So the cell builds in three safety catches — make it inactive, switch it on only where a receptor holds it, and keep inhibitors on hand to quench any that escapes. Controlled proteolysis lets a neutrophil tunnel to an infection or an osteoclast remodel bone without liquefying the neighbourhood. When that control fails, the same enzymes cut the leash for a tumour.

Clinical / real-world · MMPs and metastasis

Tumour cells hijack MMPs to chew through basal lamina and matrix and enter blood vessels — MMP over-activity correlates with invasiveness and poor prognosis, and the balance of MMPs to their inhibitors (TIMPs) is a therapeutic target. The same machinery drives normal wound healing and the tissue destruction of chronic inflammation and periodontitis.

§9.2The basal lamina (basement membrane)

Label Key — Plate 9.1
Muscle
The basal lamina wraps each muscle cell, tying it to surrounding connective tissue.
Epithelium
A sheet under the epithelial cells, separating them (apical lumen/external surface above) from the connective tissue below — the classic arrangement.
Kidney glomerulus
Sandwiched between the endothelial cell (blood side) and epithelial cell (urine side), it is the selective filter of the kidney.

The basal lamina is a thin (40–120 nm), tough, flexible sheet of matrix underlying all epithelia and wrapping individual muscle, fat and Schwann cells. Plate 9.1 shows its range of jobs: a selective filter (the kidney glomerulus), a selective barrier (letting immune cells cross while excluding fibroblasts), and a mechanical connection — in skin it binds the epidermis to the underlying dermis. It also instructs cells: setting polarity, organising membrane proteins, promoting survival/proliferation/differentiation and serving as a highway for migration.

Label Key — Plate 9.2
Laminin
The primary organiser of the sheet — self-assembles into the network that everything else builds on.
Type IV collagen
Triple-helical, rope-like fibrils forming a flexible, felt-like network — gives the basal lamina its tensile strength (this is the "network" collagen from §8.1).
Nidogen / entactin
A glycoprotein that links laminin to collagen IV, stitching the two networks together.
Perlecan
A heparan-sulfate proteoglycan (the GAG of §7) that adds charge/filtration properties.

The basal lamina is synthesised by the cells on both sides — epithelial cells contribute one set of components, connective tissue another. Plate 9.2 names the builders: laminin (the organiser of the sheet), type IV collagen (the felt-like network giving tensile strength), plus nidogen, fibronectin and the proteoglycan perlecan.

Memory hook · the two builders

"Laminin Lays out; Collagen IV is the net."

Laminin is the organiser (it even looks like a cross, laying out the plan); collagen IV is the mesh that bears the load. Nidogen ties them; perlecan adds the charged filter.

Clinical / real-world · a membrane with its own disease list

Because the glomerular basement membrane is a collagen-IV filter, antibodies against collagen IV cause Goodpasture syndrome (kidney + lung haemorrhage), and inherited collagen-IV defects cause Alport syndrome (haematuria + sensorineural deafness — the cochlea uses the same collagen). Chronically raised glucose thickens the GBM in diabetic nephropathy. And defective laminin-332 or collagen XVII at the epidermal basal lamina causes junctional epidermolysis bullosa — the skin lifts off its foundation.

R Recall checklist — the extracellular matrix (Part 3)
  • Two classes — gel-forming GAGs/proteoglycans (resist compression) + fibrous proteins (resist tension / give recoil / glue).
  • GAGs — unbranched, repeating, highly negative → draw in Na⁺ and water → compression resistance; hyaluronan, chondroitin, heparan, keratan.
  • Proteoglycans — GAGs on a core protein (all but hyaluronan); aggregates like aggrecan (>100 chains) on a hyaluronan backbone.
  • Collagen — triple helix (Gly-X-Y) → fibril → fibre; most abundant protein (~25%); types I (skin/bone), II (cartilage), IV (basal lamina net).
  • Elastin — cross-linked, stretch + recoil; aorta ~50% elastin; caged by collagen to limit over-stretch.
  • Fibronectin — the glue: binds matrix and links it (via integrins) to actin.
  • Remodelling — MMPs/proteases degrade matrix, tightly controlled (latent, receptor-confined, inhibited).
  • Basal lamina — thin sheet under all epithelia; filter/barrier/anchor/instructor; laminin + collagen IV (+ nidogen, perlecan).
§10Part 4 · junctions overview · slides 3–5

Cell junctions — the map & two superfamilies

Where the inside scaffold and the outside matrix get wired together.

The final part joins §1–§6 (cytoskeleton) to §7–§9 (matrix). Tissues come in two flavours: epithelial (packed cells, little matrix, held by junctions) and connective (few cells, abundant matrix). Epithelia are where junctions matter most — so learn the map first.

Label Key — Plate 10.1 (top → bottom, the order they occur)
Tight junction (apical)
Highest up — seals the gap between cells so nothing leaks between them (§11.4).
Cell–cell anchoring junctions
The adherens junction (ties to actin) and the desmosome (ties to intermediate filaments) — mechanical spot-welds between neighbours (§11.2–§11.3).
Channel-forming junction
The gap junction — a direct pore connecting the two cytoplasms (§11.5).
Cell–matrix anchoring junctions (basal)
The actin-linked junction (focal adhesion) and the hemidesmosome — anchor the cell down to the basal lamina (§12).
Junctional complex
The apical cluster (tight + adherens + desmosome) that rings each cell just below its apex.

Plate 10.1 is the section's spine: read an epithelial cell top to bottom and the junctions appear in a fixed order — tight → adherens → desmosome → gap → cell–matrix (actin-linked & hemidesmosome). They sort into three functional groups: occluding (tight — seal), anchoring (adherens, desmosome, hemidesmosome, actin-linked — hold), and channel-forming (gap — communicate).

Reasoning · why the apical-to-basal order is not arbitrary

The sequence follows the job. The seal (tight junction) must be highest, because its purpose is to stop fluid leaking between cells around the apex — put it any lower and apical and basal fluids would mix over the top. Below the seal come the mechanical anchors that hold neighbours together against shear, and at the very bottom the cell–matrix anchors that pin the sheet to its basal lamina foundation. Seal on top, staples in the middle, foundation bolts at the base — the same logic as building a watertight wall.

Label Key — Plate 10.2
Transmembrane adhesion protein
Spans the membrane; binds a partner outside and, via adaptors, the cytoskeleton inside. Cadherins (cell–cell) or integrins (cell–matrix).
Intracellular adaptor proteins
The plaque that couples the receptor's tail to a cytoskeletal filament — the receptor never touches the filament directly.
Cytoskeletal filaments
Actin or intermediate filaments — which one defines the junction's "type" (see the master table).
Extracellular ligand
For a cell–cell junction, the identical protein on the neighbour (homophilic); for a cell–matrix junction, an ECM protein.

All anchoring junctions share the plan in Plate 10.2 — receptor → adaptor plaque → cytoskeleton — and use one of two receptor superfamilies: cadherins for cell–cell, integrins for cell–matrix. The one table to memorise ties receptor, ligand and filament together:

The anchoring junctions — receptor, ligand, cytoskeleton
JunctionAdhesion receptorBinds to…Cytoskeleton
Adherens (cell–cell)Classical cadherinSame cadherin on neighbourActin filaments
Desmosome (cell–cell)Nonclassical cadherins (desmoglein, desmocollin)Same on neighbourIntermediate filaments
Actin-linked (cell–matrix)IntegrinECM proteinsActin filaments
Hemidesmosome (cell–matrix)Integrin (α6β4), type XVII collagenECM / basal laminaIntermediate filaments
Memory hook · the map & the pairing rule

Apical → basal: "Tight, Adherens, Desmosome, Gap, Hemidesmosome."

And the filament pairing: -somes that end in "desmo-" bind intermediate filaments (desmosome, hemidesmosome → keratin); the adherens junction and actin-linked junction bind actin. Cadherins glue cells to cells; integrins bolt cells to matrix.

§11Part 4 · cell–cell junctions · slides 6–11

Cell–cell junctions

Four ways one cell holds, seals or talks to the next.

Now each junction in turn. The three anchoring/occluding types use cadherins; the gap junction is the communicating one.

§11.1Cadherins — the principle

The primary job of cell–cell anchoring junctions is to resist forces that pull cells apart, while staying dynamic and adaptable. They are usually symmetrical and homophilic (like binds like), and highly specific. Individual cadherins bind their partner with low affinity but cluster to produce a strong "Velcro" effect; because most are cell-type specific, cells of the same type stick together and not to others. The extracellular domain mediates the homophilic binding; the intracellular domain connects (via adaptors) to cytoskeletal filaments.

Reasoning · why weak + clustered beats strong + single

If each cadherin bond were strong and permanent, tissue could never remodel — cells could not rearrange during development or wound healing. Instead the cell uses many weak bonds acting together: like Velcro, the sum is strong and load-sharing, yet individual bonds break and reform so cells can still slide and re-sort. Cell-type specificity then acts as a sorting code — homophilic cadherins let a tissue self-organise, keeping like cells together. Weakness per bond is what buys adaptability.

§11.2Adherens junctions

Label Key — Plate 11.1
Adhesion belt (zonula adherens)
In epithelia, adherens junctions fuse into a continuous belt encircling each cell, linked cell-to-cell into a tissue-wide network.
Cadherins
The homophilic receptors bridging the gap between the two adjacent membranes.
Bundle of actin filaments
The belt is tied on the inside to a ring of actin — so all cells can use their actin skeletons in a coordinated way to change tissue shape.

Adherens junctions are essential for modelling the shapes of multicellular structures — they let a whole sheet of cells use their actin rings together (e.g. to fold an epithelium into a tube). As Plate 11.1 shows, in epithelia they form a continuous adhesion belt (zonula adherens); in non-epithelial tissue they appear as small punctate/linear actin attachments; and in heart muscle they anchor the contractile actin bundles.

§11.3Desmosomes

Label Key — Plate 11.2
Nonclassical cadherins
Desmoglein and desmocollin — the desmosome's homophilic receptors across the gap.
Dense plaque of adaptor proteins
Plakoglobin, plakophilin, desmoplakin — the cytoplasmic plaque the filaments attach to.
Intermediate filaments
Keratin (in epithelia) anchored into the plaque — this is what makes a desmosome a tension-bearing rivet.

Desmosomes are structurally like adherens junctions but tie into intermediate filaments (keratin) instead of actin. They are found in mature epithelia under high mechanical stress — the epidermis and the heart — where they act as rivets distributing pulling forces across the whole cell sheet via its IF network (recall §4: IFs are the tension-bearers).

§11.4Tight junctions

Label Key — Plate 11.3
Sealing strands (claudin, occludin)
Rows of transmembrane homophilic proteins that fuse adjacent membranes into a branching seal, blocking leakage between cells.
Apical vs basolateral
The seal separates the membrane into two domains and keeps apical and basal fluids (different compositions) apart.
Directional transport (glucose)
Because nothing sneaks between cells, glucose must go through them — taken up apically and released basally to the blood.

All epithelia are anchored on one side (basal) and free on the other (apical); they are selective permeability barriers separating fluids of different composition, and that demands a seal — the tight junction, a branching network of sealing strands of transmembrane adhesion proteins (claudins, occludins). The classic example (Plate 11.3): glucose absorbed from the gut lumen must be carried through the cell to the blood, because the tight junction blocks it from slipping back between cells.

Reasoning · one seal, two payoffs

The tight junction does two jobs with one structure. As a gate it stops solutes leaking through the paracellular route, so transport must go the controlled transcellular way. As a fence it stops membrane proteins diffusing between the apical and basal surfaces, keeping (say) glucose importers apical and exporters basal. Without the fence, the pumps would scramble and vectorial transport — the whole point of an epithelium — would collapse.

§11.5Gap junctions

Label Key — Plate 11.4
Connexon
A ring of six connexin subunits forming a half-channel; two connexons (one from each cell) dock to make a continuous pore.
Channel ~1.4 nm
The pore diameter — it sets the size cut-off for what can pass.
Gap of 2–4 nm
The narrow intercellular gap the paired connexons bridge (hence "gap" junction).
Homo-/heteromeric, homo-/heterotypic
Connexons can mix connexin types (meric) and pair unlike partners (typic) — tuning what the channel passes.

Gap junctions are the communicating junction: paired connexons create a direct channel from one cytoplasm to the next. The ~1.4 nm pore passes inorganic ions and small water-soluble molecules but not macromolecules (proteins, nucleic acids). Because ions carry charge, gap junctions let cells conduct electrical signals directly — the basis of the rapid spread of action potentials across heart muscle.

Worked example · why an ion passes a gap junction but a protein cannot

The slide gives one number — a pore of ~1.4 nm. Turn it into the ~1 kDa "rule of thumb" for gap-junction permeability.

  1. The gate is size, set by the pore radius. A ~1.4 nm channel has a radius of about 0.7 nm. Only molecules whose hydrated radius is smaller than this can thread through.
  2. Size a small metabolite. Ions (Na⁺, K⁺, Ca²⁺) and small molecules like glucose or a cyclic-AMP messenger are only a few tenths of a nanometre across — comfortably under 0.7 nm. They pass.
  3. Size a protein. Even a small globular protein of ~15 kDa has a radius of roughly 1.7 nm — more than double the pore radius. It is physically excluded, as are nucleic acids.
  4. Convert to the mass cut-off. The largest thing that fits (~0.7 nm) works out to a molecular mass of about 1000 Da (1 kDa) — the standard teaching limit.

A ~1.4 nm pore ⇒ a ~1 kDa cut-off: ions and small metabolites/second messengers share freely between coupled cells, but proteins and nucleic acids stay put. That is why a gap junction couples cells electrically and metabolically without merging their identities.

Memory hook · the four cell–cell junctions

Seal · Belt · Rivet · Tunnel.

Tight = seal; Adherens = actin belt; Desmosome = keratin rivet; Gap = communicating tunnel. (Connexon = 6 connexins; pore ~1.4 nm.)

Clinical / real-world · a disease for every junction

Cadherins: loss of E-cadherin lets carcinoma cells detach and metastasise (the "epithelial–mesenchymal transition"). Desmosomes: autoantibodies to desmoglein cause pemphigus vulgaris (the epidermis blisters apart), and desmosomal-gene mutations cause arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy. Tight junctions: they build the blood–brain barrier, and their failure underlies "leaky gut" and some diarrhoeal disease. Gap junctions: connexin-43 couples cardiac myocytes for conduction (its disruption promotes arrhythmia), and connexin-26 mutations are a leading cause of congenital deafness.

§12Part 4 · cell–matrix junctions · slides 12–13

Cell–matrix junctions

Integrins — the receptors that read the matrix and wire it to the skeleton.

The last junctions bolt the cell to the ECM of §7–§9. They close the loop of the whole series: outside matrix → transmembrane receptor → inside cytoskeleton.

Label Key — Plate 12.1
Integrin (α + β subunits)
The matrix receptor: a large extracellular domain binds specific motifs in ECM proteins; a short intracellular tail binds an adaptor complex.
Talin / vinculin / kindlin
The adaptor plaque coupling the integrin tail to the actin filament — an actin-linked cell–matrix junction (focal adhesion).
Hemidesmosome
In epithelia, links the basal lamina to the cell's keratin intermediate filaments — via integrin α6β4 and collagen XVII (BP180) with plectin/BP230.

The ECM exerts a powerful influence on cells through transmembrane adhesion proteins acting as matrix receptors — chiefly integrins. As Plate 12.1 shows, a large extracellular domain binds specific amino-acid motifs in ECM proteins (the classic one is RGD), while the short intracellular tail binds an adaptor complex linking to the cytoskeleton — usually actin. These actin-linked junctions can be small and transient (the focal adhesions a crawling cell makes and breaks, §6.2) or large and durable. In epithelia, hemidesmosomes instead link the basal lamina to keratin intermediate filaments — the "half-desmosome" that bolts the cell sheet to its foundation.

Reasoning · why integrins signal both ways

An integrin is a two-way transducer. Outside-in: gripping matrix clusters integrins and assembles the adhesion plaque, telling the cell "you are anchored" — a signal that permits survival and proliferation (unanchored cells undergo anoikis, death by detachment). Inside-out: the cell can switch an integrin's affinity from within, deciding when to grip and when to let go — exactly what the migration cycle of §6.2 needs, and how a platelet activates to clot. The focal adhesion is therefore a mechanosensor: it measures matrix stiffness and tension and feeds it back to the cytoskeleton and nucleus.

Memory hook · what integrins do, and their filament

INTEGRin INTEGRates outside with inside.

Integrins bolt cell to matrix (cf. cadherins = cell to cell). Filament rule again: the actin-linked focal adhesion vs the hemidesmosome on keratin (intermediate filaments) — "desmo" = intermediate filaments, every time.

Clinical / real-world · unbolting the epithelium

Attack the hemidesmosome and skin lifts off its base: autoantibodies to collagen XVII / BP180 and BP230 cause bullous pemphigoid (tense subepidermal blisters in the elderly), and inherited defects cause junctional epidermolysis bullosa. Integrins are also central to metastasis and angiogenesis (tumours re-grip new matrix through them) and to immunity — defective β2 integrins cause leukocyte adhesion deficiency, where white cells cannot stick to vessel walls to exit into infected tissue.

R Recall checklist — cell junctions (Part 4)
  • Apical → basal order — tight → adherens → desmosome → gap → cell–matrix (actin-linked & hemidesmosome).
  • Three groups — occluding (tight/seal), anchoring (adherens, desmosome, hemidesmosome, actin-linked), channel-forming (gap).
  • Two superfamilies — cadherins (cell–cell, homophilic) & integrins (cell–matrix).
  • Filament pairing — adherens & actin-linked → actin; desmosome & hemidesmosome → intermediate filaments (keratin).
  • Cadherins — weak but clustered ("Velcro"), homophilic, cell-type specific.
  • Tight junction — claudin/occludin sealing strands; gate + fence → directional transport (gut glucose).
  • Gap junction — connexon (6 connexins), ~1.4 nm pore / ~1 kDa cut-off; electrical + metabolic coupling.
  • Integrins — bind ECM (RGD) outside, actin inside; focal adhesions = mechanosensors; inside-out & outside-in signalling.
  • Clinical — E-cadherin/metastasis, pemphigus (desmoglein), blood–brain barrier (tight), connexin deafness, bullous pemphigoid (hemidesmosome).
